source_text: Ut illis in cerimoniarum et hostiarum observatione gloriantibus, perque hoc aestimantibus alias nationes nullis legis ritibus consecratas ad consortium sui nec posse admitti subito, nec debere, diceret, quia etsi in illis observationibus fuisset summa iustitiae, haberet tamen in potestate sua Deus, quamdam facere populorum commutationem, ut reiceret quos vellet, et quos vellet assumeret. Cui sensui respondet sub persona Iudaeorum, nihil debere iam exigi ab hominis voluntate; quandoquidem Deus, cuius vult miseretur, et quem vult obdurat [n346] . Ad quod refert Apostolus: O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? [n347] Et infert testimonium prophe e Isaiae: Numquid dicit, inquit, figmentum ei qui se finxit: Utquid me fecisti sic? [n348] Additque de suo: Aut non habet potestatem figulus luti ex eadem massa facere aliud vas in honorem, aliud in contumeliam? [n349] Et est sensus eiusmodi: Quia ego commendavi voluntatem Dei, auctoritatemque gratiae eius exposui, dicens quod misericordiam praestaret, cuiuscumque misertus fuisset; tu mihi, o Iudaee, calumniam concitasti, quasi commendatio prolata a me voluntatis et potestatis divinae ad excidium iustitiae illius pertineret; et quia dixi: Facit quod vult; argumentatus es nihil iam reposci ab hominis voluntate debere, si Deus totum pro sua faceret voluntate; cum personae dignitas locum excluserit quaestionis. Nam si dixissem: Facit Deus quod debet secundum iustitiae suae leges quae de meritis iudicat singulorum; nihil quale nunc obicis, utique rettulisses; nunc vero quia dixi: Facit Deus quod vult, putasti me aliquid furatum esse de iustitiae dignitate. Utrumque igitur idem est. Nam cum de Deo dico: Facit quod vult, nihil aliud dico, quam: Facit quod debet; quia scio eum nihil aliud velle quam debet. Ubi ergo inseparabiliter voluntas cohaeret aequitati quamcumque de illis nominavero, utramque signavi.
pass_a_gloss: That to those glorying in the observation of ceremonies and of victims, and through this estimating that other nations consecrated by no rites of the law neither can be admitted suddenly to the consortium of themselves, nor ought, he would say, that even if in those observations there had been the sum of justice, nevertheless God would have in his own power, to make a certain commutation of peoples, that he would reject whom he would, and take up whom he would. To which sense he answers under the person of the Jews, that nothing ought now to be exacted from the will of a human; since indeed God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. To which the Apostle refers: O human, you who are you who answer God? And he brings in a testimony of the prophet Isaiah: Does the thing fashioned, he says, say to him who fashioned it: Why have you made me so? And he adds from his own: Or does the potter of clay not have power from the same mass to make another vessel unto honor, another unto insult? And the sense is of this kind: Because I have commended the will of God, and have expounded the authority of his grace, saying that he would furnish mercy, of whomever he had had mercy; you to me, O Jew, have stirred a calumny, as if the commendation brought forth by me of the will and power of God pertained to the destruction of that justice; and because I said: He does what he wills; you have argued that nothing now ought to be claimed back from the will of a human, if God would do the whole according to his own will; when the dignity of the person has shut out the place of the question. For if I had said: God does what he ought according to the laws of his justice which judges about the deserts of each; nothing such as you now object, at any rate you would have brought back; now however because I said: God does what he wills, you thought I had stolen something from the dignity of justice. Both therefore are the same. For when about God I say: He does what he wills, I say nothing other, than: He does what he ought; because I know him to will nothing other than he ought. Where therefore will coheres inseparably to equity, whichever of those I shall have named, I have signed both.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS meritum=desert; Blaise without later merit-system

pass_b_english: They boasted of observing ceremonies and sacrifices, and therefore supposed that other nations, consecrated by none of the Law's rites, neither could nor should suddenly be admitted to fellowship with them. He would tell them that even if the whole of righteousness had consisted in those observances, God would still have had power to make a change among the peoples, rejecting whom he wished and taking whom he wished. In answer to this meaning, a reply is made in the person of the Jews: nothing should now be demanded from the human will, since God “has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18). To this the apostle replies: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). He introduces the prophet Isaiah's testimony: “Does what is molded say to the one who molded it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (Isaiah 45:9; Romans 9:20). He adds in his own words: “Does the potter not have power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:21).

The meaning is this: “Because I commended God's will and explained the authority of his grace, saying that he grants mercy to whomever he has mercy on, you, O Jew, raised a false accusation against me. You acted as though my commendation of divine will and power involved the destruction of divine justice. Because I said, ‘He does what he wills’, you argued that nothing should any longer be demanded of human will if God does everything according to his own will. Yet the dignity of the person concerned left no room for that objection. If I had said, ‘God does what he ought, according to the laws of his justice which judges each person's deserts’, you certainly would not have raised the objection you now raise. But because I said, ‘God does what he wills’, you thought I had stolen something from justice's dignity. Both statements, then, mean the same thing. When I say of God, ‘He does what he wills’, I say nothing other than, ‘He does what he ought’, because I know that he wills nothing other than what he ought. Where will is inseparably joined to fairness, whichever of them I name, I have indicated both.”
